canonical_data: a per-connection credential vault, an agent backend database (memory, skills, tasks), and published artifacts, held on the user's own machine or VPC when self-hosted, or in MindsDB's hosted console
current_repo_note: This repository is a superproject: its top-level MIT LICENSE covers only the build/glue code. It pins four Git submodules, each under its own license, reviewed here at the exact commits mindshub's main branch pins: frontend (mindsdb/cowork) is AGPL-3.0; backend/core_agent (mindsdb/anton) is MIT; backend/core_api (mindsdb/cowork-server) -- the agent backend the whole product depends on to run -- carries an all-rights-reserved proprietary notice with no reuse grant; and backend/data-vault (mindsdb/data-vault, the MindsDB core engine) splits Elastic License 2.0 for its core against MIT for its `/mindsdb/integrations` subdirectory. The taxonomy has no dedicated id for Elastic License 2.0, so it is recorded here as LicenseRef-Commercial (source-available with reuse and hosting restrictions), the same bucket other Atlas records use for comparable dual-licensed cores. The README's own 'released under the MIT License' framing describes only the top-level repository, not the product a user actually runs.
strengths: Connects a wide, named set of data sources (BigQuery, Postgres, Gmail, Drive, HubSpot, Notion, Linear) through a scoped credential vault, rather than one narrow integration
Model access and agent harness are both swappable: a router across Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi, and interchangeable open-source harnesses (Anton, Hermes) selectable from a dropdown
High adoption signal (39.7k stars, pushed within the last day) and a documented path to deploy on-prem, air-gapped, or in a private VPC rather than only the hosted console
weaknesses: The agent backend that executes the whole workspace (backend/core_api, i.e. mindsdb/cowork-server) is licensed all-rights-reserved at the commit this repository pins, so the 'run on your machine, in your VPC' claim depends on a component the operator cannot inspect, modify, or redistribute
No approval-gate, audit-trail, or session-recovery mechanism is documented in the README; human-control and observability claims cannot be established from the evidence reviewed here

The repository itself ships no application code: it is a superproject of four separately licensed submodules, so behavior claims rest on the submodules' own (unreviewed-in-depth) documentation rather than this repository's content
why_it_matters: A widely starred example of a vendor packaging a broad, connected-data agent workspace as an ostensibly open-source superproject whose actual operational core is proprietary, which matters for any reader evaluating it on the top-level MIT badge alone.
